parole.significato: A tropical American evergreen shrub, Bixa orellana; the lipstick tree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish achiote, from Classical Nahuatl āchiyōtl.

parole.significato: Paper produced from the bark of adult Ficus trees.
parole.testo: From Spanish (papel) amate (“amate paper”), from Classical Nahuatl āmatl (“paper”).

parole.significato: Any of various parts of the Agave (or similar) plants, when used as soap.
parole.testo: From Mexican Spanish amole, from Classical Nahuatl ahmōlli.

parole.significato: A sweetened thick drink or thin gruel made from cornmeal, served hot.
parole.testo: From Spanish atole, from Classical Nahuatl ātōlli.

parole.significato: The large, usually yellowish-green or black, savory fruit of the avocado tree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin American Spanish avocado, from the earlier aguacate, which comes from Classical Nahuatl āhuacatl (“avocado”). Doublet of abacate. Compare aguacatillo, avocadillo. The first mention can be found in a catalogue of Jamaican plants in 1696.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Mexica people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish azteca, from Classical Nahuatl aztēcah, plural of aztēcatl (“inhabitant of Aztlán”).

parole.significato: A tree, Theobroma cacao, whose seed is used to make chocolate.
parole.testo: From Spanish cacao, from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl. Doublet of cocoa.

parole.significato: Any member of the species Bassariscus sumichrasti, an arboreal relative of the racoon (and other procyonids).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish cacomixtle, itself borrowed from Classical Nahuatl tlahcomiztli.

parole.significato: A floating island composed of Pontederia plants.
parole.testo: From Spanish camalote, from Classical Nahuatl camalotl.

parole.significato: sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas)
parole.testo: From Spanish camote, from Classical Nahuatl camohtli. Compare Tagalog kamote.

parole.significato: The Mexican cherry (Prunus serotina subsp. capuli, once Prunus capollin) and Prunus capuli, that yields a sap used in n…
parole.testo: From Spanish capulín, from Classical Nahuatl capolin.

parole.significato: A mockingbird.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish cenzontle, from Classical Nahuatl centzontleh, shortened form of centzontlahtōleh (“mockingbird”, literally “possessor of four hundred words”), from centzontli (“four hundred, a count of four hundred”) + tlahtōlli (“language, word, statement”) + -eh (“possessor of”).

parole.significato: Any of several cracid birds, of the genus Ortalis, limited to the Americas, that resemble the guans.
parole.testo: Late 19th century. From South American Spanish chachalaca, from Classical Nahuatl chachalacani (“tattler, gossiper”), from chāchalāni (“to make a hubbub, create an uproar”).

parole.significato: Sicyos edulis, a tropical American perennial herbaceous vine having tendrils, tuberous roots, and a green, pear-shaped…
parole.testo: From Spanish chayote, from Classical Nahuatl chayohtli.

parole.significato: A Mexican sage grown for its edible seeds, Salvia hispanica.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish chía, from Classical Nahuatl chiyan (“seed of the chia plant”).

parole.significato: A traditional Mexican dish of fried tortilla chips topped with salsa.
parole.testo: From Spanish chilaquiles, from Classical Nahuatl chīlātl.

parole.significato: The pungent, spicy fresh or dried fruit of any of several cultivated varieties of capsicum peppers, used in cooking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish chile, from Classical Nahuatl chīlli.

parole.significato: A floating island in a shallow lake bed, upon which crops were grown.
parole.testo: From Spanish chinampa, from Classical Nahuatl chināmitl (“cane fence”).

parole.significato: A ripe jalapeño pepper, dried and smoked for use in cooking.
parole.testo: From Spanish chipotle, from Classical Nahuatl chīlpōctli, compound of chīlli (“pepper”) + pōctli (“smoke”).

parole.significato: A food made from ground roasted cocoa beans.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl, of uncertain origin. See that entry for more information.

parole.significato: The dried and partially fermented fatty seeds of the cacao tree from which chocolate is made.
parole.testo: From Spanish cacao, from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl. The form cocoa came about by confusion with coco, popularized by Samuel Johnson's A Dictionary of the English Language. Doublet of cacao.

parole.significato: A resinous exudation from various tropical trees, especially Hymenaea courbaril and Schinus terebinthifolia, used chief…
parole.testo: From Spanish copal, from Classical Nahuatl copalli (“incense”).

parole.significato: Corn (maize) harvested before reaching full maturity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish elote (“fresh ear of corn”).

parole.significato: A pungent herb used in Latin-American cooking and tea making, and in folk medicine; Dysphania ambrosioides.
parole.testo: From Spanish epazote, from Classical Nahuatl epazōtl.

parole.significato: An avocado-based greenish dip with onions, tomato, and spices, common to Mexican cuisine and often served with tortilla…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish guacamole, from Classical Nahuatl āhuacamōlli (from āhuacatl (“avocado”) + mōlli (“sauce; broth”)).

parole.significato: An edible seed of Leucaena esculenta.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish guaje, from Classical Nahuatl huāxin.

parole.significato: A traditional blouse worn by the women of various indigenous peoples of Central America including the Maya and Zapotec,…
parole.testo: From Spanish huipil, from Classical Nahuatl huīpīlli (“woman's blouse”).

parole.significato: Corn smut prepared as a delicacy.
parole.testo: From Spanish huitlacoche, an alteration of cuitlacoche, from Classical Nahuatl cuitlacochin.

parole.significato: A variety of Agave angustifolia var. angustifolia (syn. Agave rigida), furnishing a strong coarse fiber.
parole.testo: American Spanish, from Classical Nahuatl ichtli.

parole.significato: A mombin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish jocote, from Classical Nahuatl.

parole.significato: An Aztec obsidian sword or club.
parole.testo: From Spanish macuahuitl, from Classical Nahuatl māccuahuitl.

parole.significato: A member of an indigenous people of the Americas
parole.testo: From Spanish mexica, from Classical Nahuatl mēxihcah, absolutive plural form of mēxihcatl (“Mexica, Aztec”).

parole.significato: A cyclical crop-growing system used throughout Mesoamerica.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish milpa, from Classical Nahuatl.

parole.significato: A member of a Mesoamerican people who live primarily in southern Mexico.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mixteco, alteration of mixteca, from Classical Nahuatl mixtēcah (“Mixtecs”, plural).

parole.significato: A traditional Mexican stone tool, equivalent in function to a mortar and pestle, used for grinding food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish molcajete, from Classical Nahuatl mōlcaxitl.

parole.significato: Any of several spicy sauces typical of the cuisine of Mexico and neighboring Central America countries, especially one…
parole.testo: From Spanish mole, from Classical Nahuatl mōlli (“sauce; stew; something ground”).

parole.significato: An animal form which a person may take.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish nahual, from Classical Nahuatl nāhualli (“sorcerer, spirit, animal form a person may take”).

parole.significato: A member of a group of people indigenous to Central Mexico, spanning multiple tribal groups and including the Aztecs.
parole.testo: From Spanish náhuatl, from Classical Nahuatl nahuatl, nahuatlatolli (“the clear or understandable language”).

parole.significato: An interpreter in an indigenous language, not necessarily Nahuatl.
parole.testo: From Spanish nahuatlato, from Nahuatl nāhuatlahtoh.

parole.significato: A large shrub or small tree of subtropical and tropical areas of the Americas, Byrsonima crassifolia, bearing a small,…
parole.testo: From American Spanish nance, from Classical Nahuatl.

parole.significato: A prickly pear cactus from the genus Opuntia, especially Opuntia cochinellifera; the edible pads (fleshy leaves) of the…
parole.testo: From Spanish nopal, from Classical Nahuatl nohpalli (“Opuntia cactus”). Compare nopales.

parole.significato: A semihard white cheese from the Oaxaca region of Mexico.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish Oaxaca, from Classical Nahuatl Huāxyacac, from Huāxacatzin (“name of a hill”), from huāxin (huaje) (Leucaena leucocephala) + yacatl (“nose”) + -tzin (“honorific suffix”).

parole.significato: A person belonging to the indigenous Otomi ethnic group of central Mexico.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish otomí, from Classical Nahuatl otomih, plural of otomitl.

parole.significato: A small, spineless cactus (Lophophora williamsii) found from southwest United States to central Mexico that produces bu…
parole.testo: From Spanish peyote, from Classical Nahuatl peyotl.

parole.significato: A darkling beetle of the genus Eleodes, endemic to the Sonoran Desert and adjacent regions, and known for its defensive…
parole.testo: From Mexican Spanish pinacate, from Classical Nahuatl pinacatl (“black beetle”).

parole.significato: A coarse flour made from ground toasted maize kernels, often mixed with herbs, which may be eaten by itself or incorpor…
parole.testo: From Mexican Spanish pinole, from Classical Nahuatl pinolli (“flour, ground maize or chia”).

parole.significato: A traditional Mexican soup, made from hominy, pork, chilli and other ingredients.
parole.testo: From Spanish pozole, from Classical Nahuatl pozolli (“stew of maize kernels”).

parole.significato: Any trogon of the genus Pharomacrus, especially a resplendent quetzal (Pharomacrus mocinno), which has very long tail f…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish quetzal, from Classical Nahuatl quetzalli (“brightly colored tail feather, quetzal feather”), from quetza (“to raise, lift”); see also Classical Nahuatl quetzaltōtōtl (“quetzal bird”).

parole.significato: Any of several species of North American desert plants of the genus Dasylirion, of the asparagus family.
parole.testo: From Mexican Spanish sotol, from Classical Nahuatl zōtolin (“palm tree”).

parole.significato: one-eighth of a Mexican real (issued until 1897)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish tlaco (“tlaco”), from Classical Nahuatl tlaco (“half”).

parole.significato: Angel's trumpet, an annual plant of species Datura inoxia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish toloache, from Classical Nahuatl toloatzin, from toloa (“to bow the head”) + tzin (reverential). Doublet of toloatzin.

parole.significato: A plant of the nightshade family originating in Mexico, Physalis philadelphica, cultivated for its tomato-like green to…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish tomatillo, diminutive of tomate (“tomato”), ultimately from Classical Nahuatl tomatl.

parole.significato: A widely cultivated plant, Solanum lycopersicum, having edible fruit.
parole.testo: Variant of earlier tomate, from Spanish tomate, from Classical Nahuatl tomatl, from Proto-Nahuan *toma-tl. Compare tomatillo.

parole.significato: Any of a number of large freshwater sedges of western North America formerly classified in the genus Scirpus, but now m…
parole.testo: From Spanish tule, from Classical Nahuatl tōllin (“bulrush, sedge”).

parole.significato: A Mexican and Central American tree (Castilla elastica), related to the breadfruit tree, whose milky juice contains cao…
parole.testo: From Spanish hule, from Classical Nahuatl ōlli.

parole.significato: A prickly pear cactus of species Opuntia matudae, native to Central Mexico.
parole.testo: From Spanish xoconostle, from Classical Nahuatl xoconōchtli (“sour prickly-pear”).

parole.significato: A breed of dog, the Mexican Hairless.
parole.testo: Through Spanish from Classical Nahuatl xoloitzcuintli (literally “dog of Xolotl”).

parole.significato: A member of a Native American indigenous group who inhabited most of what is now the state of Zacatecas and the northea…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish zacateco.

parole.significato: A New World vulture of the family Cathartidae, especially the black vulture (Coragyps atratus).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish zopilote, from Classical Nahuatl tzopīlōtl.
